newsitem.title: GERMANY: German watchdog steps up fight against crime.
newsitem.headline: German watchdog steps up fight against crime.

text.p: Germany's fledgling securities watchdog said on Tuesday it had become more efficient in uncovering insider trading and had expanded its surveillance activities to firms operating in the grey market.

The Frankfurt-based Federal Supervisory Authority for Securities Trading (BaWe) also urged regulators to set rules for securities trading on the Internet and added its voice to calls for German firms to adopt a voluntary takeover code.
BaWE president Georg Wittich told a news conference the office had established a good track record in its most high-profile task -- preventing insider trading.

The office, which also ensures companies report market-sensitive news on time, passed on 15 cases of suspected insider dealing to public prosecutors in the first half of 1997, marking a clear increase from the previous year, he said.
The increase did not reveal a rise in the incidence of insider trading in Germany, but rather greater BaWe efficiency.
"Certainly we have gained experience in the past two and a half years," he said. "I believe we have a good system here."

Insider deals were criminalised for the first time in Germany in mid-1994 as part of a package of reforms -- widely viewed as long overdue -- intended to bring the country's investor protection measures up to international standards.
The BAWe, the linchpin of Germany's drive to put a stop to insider deals, was equipped in 1996 with an electronic trading surveillance system to process 80 million trading reports.
In an expansion of its activities, the office said it was gearing up to turn attention in 1998 to some 7,500 unregulated investment firms thought to be operating in Germany.
The passage into German law of a European directive on investment services enabled the BAWe to tackle this segment which has not been subject to official supervision until now.
"This is a very significant expansion of our activities," Wittich told the news conference.

Wittich has repeatedly voiced concern at the activities of these unregulated firms, which operate mainly over the telephone and are thought to have caused major losses to the tens of thousands of German investors who bought up the "penny stocks" and other products which such firms offer.
The BAWe, which now has just under 100 staff, would need "significant" additional personnel and office space to cope with its enlarged activities, Wittich said.

Turning to the issue of takeovers, the BaWe joined the German government and bourse officials in urging German companies to abide by a voluntary takeover code -- warning that the consequence of further rejection could be a takeover law.
Wittich said the lack of agreement on a takeover code in Germany constituted a significant disadvantage for investors.
"There is clearly an acceptance problem," he said.
The German bourse introduced the voluntary takeover code in October 1995. Yet the code has so far found the support of only 270 of a total of 683 listed companies.
Just 61 of the DAX-100 companies have pledged to abide by the bourse's rules and six DAX-30 companies have yet to agree.

Under the terms of the gentlemen's agreement, a company that owns a stake of more than 50 percent in a target company has 18 months to make an offer to outstanding shareholders, except in instances where an exemption has been granted.
Turning to wider issues, the watchdog called on international regulators to draw up rules for securities trading over the Internet to prevent abuse of the system.
"It is not our intention to abandon the Internet - that would not be realistic," he said. "But we do not have much time. We must act quickly."
